identity: This is a deliberately tiny test fixture, not a production system: a 13-file, 255-line multi-language 'solution' committed inside the analyzer's own test suite. Its job is to exercise the analyzer engine across every tree-sitter language it supports (Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust, Ruby, Swift, JavaScript) and across the main component and relationship types, and to anchor the P4-1 parity snapshot that the P4-7 cutover diffs against. The 'services' do nothing real; each exists to trigger a specific detection path.
audience: Maintainers of the analyzer itself, reading the map to verify that the engine detected what the fixture was built to make detectable. They open it asking 'did the parser see the FastAPI port bind, the compose services, the Go main.go, the Swift package?' — the map is a test oracle, not an orientation aid for newcomers. (Inferred: the README addresses analyzer developers, not users of polyglot.)
what_matters: Complete per-language coverage: every one of the seven code languages plus the config formats must appear, because a missing language is an engine regression, not a small system
Correct component typing per detection path (api-server from port bind, database/cache from compose, package from manifests) — each component exists to test one classifier
The single declared relationship (web calls the API over HTTP) being present, since it is the fixture's only cross-component edge
Stability against the parity snapshot: any drift in the map is a diff the P4-7 cutover must explain
Fidelity to the README's layout list, which is the fixture's own specification

criteria.statement: The map names every language-bearing component the README lists (api, web, worker, core, rubylib, ios, compose db and cache) and assigns each its correct language and manifest, because each one exists solely to prove a parser path works.
criteria.why: A production map can tolerate a missed minor library; here a missing Ruby or Swift component means a tree-sitter integration silently failed, which is the exact regression this fixture exists to catch.
criteria.how_to_check: Compare the map's component list against the README's Layout section item by item, checking language and manifest file (pyproject.toml, package.json, go.mod, Cargo.toml, Gemfile, Package.swift, docker-compose.yml) for each.

criteria.statement: The web-to-API HTTP call is represented as the system's one inter-service relationship, and no invented relationships appear alongside it.
criteria.why: The fixture has exactly one deliberate cross-component edge; it is the relationship-detection test case. Hallucinated extra edges are as much a failure here as a missed one, because the parity snapshot diffs on this.
criteria.how_to_check: Look at the relationship list: it should contain the web-client-to-services/api HTTP edge and nothing between components the README does not connect.

criteria.statement: Every component's map entry describes it as a fixture exercising a detection path, never as a real product capability (no invented business purpose for the worker, the Rust lib, or the iOS app).
criteria.why: The code bodies are near-empty stubs; any prose implying real functionality is fabrication, and this subject is the easiest place to catch a rung inventing plausible-sounding purpose.
criteria.how_to_check: Read each component description and ask whether it claims behaviour beyond what a ~20-line stub file could contain; check descriptions against the actual source lines.

criteria.statement: Component types match their triggering signal: services/api is typed by its port bind, compose/db and compose/cache by their docker-compose declarations, services/worker by main.go, the libraries by their manifests.
criteria.why: Type classification is per-signal here; a compose service typed as a code module or a library typed as a service means a classifier crossed wires, which matters far more in this fixture than the type label itself would elsewhere.
criteria.how_to_check: For each component, confirm the stated type against its source of truth: docker-compose.yml for db/cache, the port-binding code in services/api, entry-file convention for the worker, manifest kind for each package.

criteria.statement: The map states, prominently, that this is a CI test fixture rather than a deployable system, and its overview does not read like a startup's architecture.
criteria.why: The mechanical description already truncates to a sentence that sounds like a product ('multi-language solution'); a reader who misses the fixture framing will misjudge every downstream signal, including the zone-of-uselessness finding.
criteria.how_to_check: Read the map's top-level summary: does it say 'test fixture for the analyzer suite' in the first sentence, and does it mention the parity-snapshot role?

criteria.statement: Every enrichment target reached a terminal contract state.
criteria.why: An item still asking to climb is unfinished work, and a run that reports done over unfinished work is the failure mode the census exists to make visible.
criteria.how_to_check: The census has no items in the escalate state.

criteria.statement: Claims are grounded in evidence that checks out.
criteria.why: A claim without evidence you can point at is not an answer, and a form scorer cannot tell the difference.
criteria.how_to_check: The grounded fraction of the census, and the adjudicator's spot-check disagreement rate.

criteria.statement: What could not be established is visible as an honest gap, with a reason a reader can act on.
criteria.why: An honest map says what it does not know. A gap papered over with a plausible sentence is worse than a gap.
criteria.how_to_check: Every honest-gap item carries a non-empty reason.

weighting_adjustments: Spend almost nothing on deep per-component enrichment: the components are stubs and their mechanical descriptions plus README lines already say everything true about them. Effort beyond confirming type, language, and manifest is fabrication risk, not value.

The mechanical ranking puts services/api first on fan-in, but for this subject breadth beats depth: equal light coverage of all ten components serves the test-oracle audience better than a rich writeup of the API stub.
The 'root' component ranked band 1 with 15 commits is just the fixture's top directory absorbing all git activity; do not treat its churn as significance.
Cheapest-rung work suffices throughout; escalation on any component of this fixture is almost certainly wasted spend.
idiom_warnings: The 'zone of uselessness' finding on services/web/src is by design: nothing consumes the web client because the fixture only needs the outbound HTTP edge to exist. It is not dead code to flag.

Zero commits on nearly every component is expected — the fixture was committed as a snapshot and deliberately kept frozen so the P4-1 parity baseline stays stable; low churn signals correctness here, not abandonment.
'root' is listed as an entry point 'because it listens on a port' — that is the compose file's port declarations attributed to the root directory, not a server at the repo root.
Component and file bodies are intentionally minimal ('Keep it tiny... must parse fast in CI'); trivial-looking stub implementations are the spec, not laziness.
Names like polyglot-api and polyglot-core mimic a product naming convention purely so manifest-name detection has something realistic to parse; they do not indicate a shared product line.
